subject: Choosing landmark spacing (distance bins) for camera trap distance sampling

messages.author: d2e6f7c70e669ae3
messages.subject: Choosing landmark spacing (distance bins) for camera trap distance sampling
parts:
Hi group,

I am attempting to distance sample for wild sheep using time-lapse game cameras.  All cameras will simultaneously take pictures every 15 minutes, and I intend to put out measured marks (fence posts) in each camera view so that counts of animals can be pooled into distance bins.

My question is, would it be better to put the landmarks out linearly, (i.e. every 5 or 10 meters), or would it be better to place them out at distances that would make the area increase linearly?  One thing to note is that this situation is similar to point sampling, except that the area gained with increasing radius is not proportional to a gain in a full pi*r^2 , but pi*r^2*(42/360), because the field of view of the camera is only 42 degrees.  

In my example, If I were to put out 8 landmarks, I can either put them out at distances 5-40 in 5m increments, or I can put them out so that area increases linearly which would make the spacing look more like (5.4, 8.1, 10.8, 13.6, 16.3, 19...etc).

Also, I could not find any suggestions for determining an adequate number of bins.  Is there a decision criterion for this?  Ideally I would like to minimize the number of bins perhaps maybe to 4, if feasible.  

Best regards,

messages.subject: Re: {Suspected Spam} [distance-sampling] Choosing landmark spacing (distance bins) for camera trap distance sampling
parts:
Interesting question.

Thinking about the placement of landmarks strictly from the perspective of fitting a detection function.  I believe the landmark posts will effectively become the cutpoints of the bins for the radial distances.  In this situation, I would suggest having a larger rather than a smaller number of bins; more like 8 bins rather than 4.  Remember this is the number of points of support you will have for assessing goodness of fit of your detection function model to data.

In addition, I would encourage you to perhaps have the landmarks more closely spaced near the cameras, with increasing separation at large distances; much like your suggestion of making landmark separation similar to distance band areas.  Having a number of landmark bands close to the camera gives the opportunity to closely examine the fit of the model to your data at the place where fit is most critical--namely close to distance zero.
